Maladaptive Strategies.value: make sure to stay close to exit
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

vignette: Elias Vance was thirty-four when the dust finally settled, but the memory of that day in the war zone still moves through him like a live wire. A European-American relief worker, he had been moving crates of medical supplies through a crowded compound when the ground shuddered. A mortar struck the adjacent warehouse, showering the concrete floor with shattered glass and twisted rebar. For three minutes, he was pinned behind a toppled supply cart, the air thick with choking powder, unable to shift without risking the falling debris. The sudden collapse of open space and the rush of fine dust taught him to treat proximity as potential entrapment. When he returned to the United States, that narrow, suffocating moment did not fade; it simply changed address. At first, the alertness showed up in quiet moments. While standing in his own kitchen, Elias found himself braced, his shoulders tight even though the walls were solid and the windows were intact. He was certain that danger could breach any threshold, and he began scanning for exits the moment he crossed any doorway. In the fire station, where he worked alongside colleagues and responded to calls, this habit became routine. When stepping onto the station's polished floor, his eyes traced the perimeter, mapping every stairwell, heavy door, and loading bay. He positioned himself near the main entrance during briefings, favoring the seat with a clear line of sight and a direct path to the outside. The habit persisted through months of shifts; his bunk and the station's gear room felt like temporary shelters rather than workplaces. The war zone had taught him to read movement and intent, and that translation followed him into everyday life. When a neighbor or a passerby approached him on the sidewalk, Elias felt a quiet tightening in his chest. He was not afraid of the people themselves, but of their proximity, of what might happen if a stranger stepped too close without warning. At home, his wife, Clara, would reach for his arm, and he would steady himself, waiting for her to stop before relaxing. Positive moments, too, felt precarious. When a shift went without incident or Clara shared a quiet laugh over dinner, he would push away the warmth, certain that letting himself settle would leave him exposed. He avoided exercise; the elevated heartbeat during a run or a weight session felt too much like the racing pulse he had known in the compound. He preferred to sit with his arms folded, watching the room, rather than push through the physical exertion. Over the months, these adjustments accumulated. He missed two group calisthenics sessions, citing equipment checks instead. At home, he kept the study door propped open and slept with his side of the bed facing the hallway, so he could rise without turning his back to the rest of the house. His marriage remained steady, but the distance was subtle; Clara learned not to surprise him, and he stopped suggesting weekend hikes, preferring short, predictable drives. The fire station became his anchor and his testing ground. During roll calls, he stayed near the bay doors, listening to the dispatcher's voice while his eyes tracked the yard. When a rookie firefighter clapped him on the shoulder after a successful drill, Elias nodded, thanked him, and subtly shifted his weight toward the exit. He was not withdrawing from his work or his life; he was simply conserving his vigilance, treating every room, every street, and every quiet evening as a space where the ground might shudder again. Now, after nearly two years of living with the quiet hum of alertness, Elias has come to the clinic. He says he is here; the constant scanning has begun to fray his focus, and he is tired of bracing. What he hopes for is not the complete disappearance of the tension, but a way to carry it without it governing his steps. What frightens him most is the thought that if he stops watching, if he lets his guard down completely, the compound will close around him once more. He sits in the waiting room with his shoes on, his back to the wall, eyes resting on the double doors, ready to step forward when the moment feels safe enough to do so.
